newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Canada says WTO to seek ways to help poor countries.
newsitem.headline: Canada says WTO to seek ways to help poor countries.

text.p: A Canadian call for a meeting in the New Year to look at ways to help poorer countries make the most of their trade opportunities was accepted by the World Trade Organisation, Trade Minister Art Eggleton said on Friday.
He said the idea had been incorporated into a plan of action adopted by the WTO, which sets rules on international trade, at its ministerial meeting in Singapore this week.
The plan aims at improving investments and market conditions for least developed countries (LLDCs) and developing countries.

"It also deals with a Canadian proposal that a meeting be held early in the new year...to foster an integrated approach assisting these countries in enhancing their trade opportunities," Eggleton said.
Other bodies involved will include the United Nations Conference on Trade and Development, international aid agencies and multilateral financial institutions.
Asked about tax concessions to developing countries, such as zero tariffs for textiles and clothing, Eggleton said: "That's got considerable sensitivity for Canadian domestic industry."
He added there was already an agreement on textiles and clothing, and a quota system in place.
He said all 128 WTO members agreed to the conference's final declaration, which contained a reference to the textile agreement, including developing and least developed countries.
"There is an agreement on textiles and clothing and we are honouring that agreement. To change that course opens up difficulty with respect to preservation of jobs back home," the minister said.
But the talks were criticised by some for being too focused on achieving agreement on an information technology pact, and not enough on issues affecting poorer countries.

"On textiles and clothing, our assessment was below par," said Pakistan's minister for trade, Mohammad Zubair Khan, said earlier, adding that Pakistan agreed to compromise on the declaration's wording only after assurances that improvements will be made later.
